sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source belongs to a high-angle reverse fault system that is hypothesized to border the northern flank of the Hyblean Plateau. A segment of this fault system is included in this Database as an Individual Seismogenic Source. The geometry of this source is based on geological and geomorphologic observations on the northern sector of the Hyblean Mts., and in particular on the Monte Lauro ridge.
According to the literature, the morphology of the Hyblean plateau is delineated by large normal fault systems that separate it from the Gela-Catania foredeep to the west and northwest, and from the Ionian basin to the east. To the north the Hyblean Plateau is paralleled by a NE-trending depression commonly referred to as Scordia-Lentini graben.
The structural and tectonic interpretation proposed by this Database implies that the northern margin of the Hyblean plateau is characterized by active compressional structures, and that the extensional structures could have been reactivated with a reverse sense of motion in the current tectonic regime. The reverse/thrust kinematics of the Individual and Composite Seismogenic sources bordering to the north and to the south the Catania Plain (i.e the easternmost outcropping portion of the Gela-Catania foredeep) is in agreement with geological observations and present-day stress field and GPS data, which show NNW-directed active shortening between the Hyblean Plateau and Mt. Etna.
The seismogenic sources found along the northern margin of the Catania Plain belong to the eastern Apennines-Maghrebide thrust system cropping out in Sicily between Gela and Catania. This S-verging fold-and-thrust belt developed since early Miocene times in the framework of the ~N-S directed Africa-Europe plate convergence. The outermost and most recent thrust front of the Maghrebian thrust belt forms a broad south convex arch, running for most of its length off the southern Sicilian coast. This front crops out on-shore only in its eastern portion between Gela and Catania.
The normal fault system bordering to the south the Catania Plain, that now is thought to be reactivated with a reverse sense of motion, probably formed as a consequence of the bend of the foreland lithosphere beneath the Apennines-Maghrebide chain.
Historical and instrumental catalogues (Boschi et al., 2000; Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004; Pondrelli et al., 2006; Guidoboni et al., 2007) show significant seismicity that can be associated with this Composite Seismogenic Source, concentrated mainly near the northern margin of the Hyblean Plateau. The largest earthquakes that struck in this area are the 4 February 1169 (Mw 6.6), the 10 December 1542 (Mw 6.6) and the 11 January 1693 (Mw 7.4) events (all magnitudes from Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004).
Two Individual Sources in this Database have been associated with the 11 January 1693 earthquake, the largest event listed in the Italian earthquake catalogue. The mainshock of the 1693 earthquake is likely to have included two or more subevents, as suggested by the existence of two separate concentrations of higher damage, but this hypothesis is not explicitly backed up by the available historical sources. The compilers of the DISS database hypotesized that this earthquake was a complex earthquake, with two shocks being caused by distinct compressional faults located to the north and to the south of the Catania Plain, respectively.
In contrast, the 1169 and the 1542 earthquakes are not associated with any Individual Seismogenic Source.
The strike of this Source was taken from the general orientation of mapped tectonic structures. The dip was based on regional geological considerations. The rake was assumed to be representative of thrusting with a right-lateral component of motion, based on general geodynamic considerations. The minimum and maximum depth were based on geometrical considerations concerning the thickness of the seismogenic layer. The slip rate was inferred from regional geodynamic observations.
